record.context_brief: True prosoluble analogue of Grothendieck's problem
record.original_question: Let Γ and ∆ be residually soluble groups and let ψ: Γ -> ∆ be a homomorphism such that the induced map on true prosoluble completions PS(ψ): PS(Γ) -> PS(∆) is an isomorphism. Determine how far ψ can fail to be an isomorphism, and in particular what additional hypotheses on Γ and ∆, such as finite generation or finite presentation, force ψ itself to be an isomorphism.

evidence.quote: Our main interest in this paper is the prosoluble analogue of Grothendieck’s problem. More precisely, let again Γ, ∆ be two groups and ψ : Γ −→ ∆ a homomorphism, but assume now that the groups are residually soluble. Assume that, at the true prosoluble level, the corresponding homomorphism PS(ψ) : PS(Γ) −→ PS(∆) is an isomorphism. How far from an isomorphism can ψ be? Additional requirements can be added on Γ and ∆ (such as finite generation, finite presentation, ...).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let Γ be a group. Define the true prosoluble completion PS(Γ) of Γ as the inverse limit of the inverse system of all soluble quotients of Γ (equivalently, the inverse limit of Γ/N as N ranges over the normal subgroups of Γ with Γ/N soluble). A group Γ is called residually soluble if the natural map Γ → PS(Γ) is injective, equivalently if the intersection of all normal subgroups N ⊴ Γ with Γ/N soluble is trivial.

Any homomorphism ψ: Γ → Δ between groups induces a continuous homomorphism PS(ψ): PS(Γ) → PS(Δ) of topological groups.

Problem. Suppose Γ and Δ are residually soluble groups and ψ: Γ → Δ is a homomorphism such that PS(ψ): PS(Γ) → PS(Δ) is an isomorphism of topological groups. 

(a) Must ψ itself be an isomorphism? If not, exhibit pairs (Γ, Δ, ψ) for which PS(ψ) is an isomorphism but ψ is not, and quantify how far ψ can be from an isomorphism.

(b) Under what additional hypotheses on Γ and Δ — for instance, finite generation, finite presentation, or further finiteness/structural properties — does the assumption that PS(ψ) is an isomorphism force ψ to be an isomorphism?
artifact.status_search_result: The general problem appears partially resolved: examples of pairs of non-isomorphic residually soluble groups with isomorphic true prosoluble completions are known, answering the basic prosoluble analogue of Grothendieck's question in the negative. However, the refined question — identifying additional hypotheses (e.g. finite presentation) under which the induced isomorphism on prosoluble completions forces an isomorphism of the underlying groups — remains the subject of ongoing research, with related results in the finitely generated/finitely presented setting (e.g. on the solvable genus of free and surface groups) appearing in the literature.

status_evidence.title: The true prosoluble completion of a group: Examples and open problems
status_evidence.snippet: Examples of pairs of non-isomorphic residually soluble groups with isomorphic true prosoluble completions are exhibited.
status_evidence.claim: The prosoluble analogue of Grothendieck's question has been answered in the negative by explicit examples, while refined versions remain open.

status_evidence.title: The finite and solvable genus of finitely generated free and surface groups
status_evidence.snippet: Investigates the solvable genus, i.e. groups sharing the same set of soluble quotients with a given group.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work continues to investigate when prosoluble-completion data determines a finitely generated group up to isomorphism, indicating the refined problem is still active.

status_evidence.title: Grothendieck's problems concerning profinite completions and representations of groups
status_evidence.snippet: Bridson–Grunewald gave finitely presented residually finite groups with proper inclusions inducing isomorphisms of profinite completions.
status_evidence.claim: The analogous profinite Grothendieck problem was resolved negatively, providing the template for the prosoluble version.
